2. Use a doubly linked list to identify head and tail.

Now suppose multiple go routines access the cache:
Even GET modifies the linked list because it changes recency.
Therefore a simple implementation can protect the entire cache:
RWMutex doesn't automatically help much because successful reads
modify LRU order. They're logically reads but structurally writes.
Suppose we have 100 million cached object but one machine can only
handle 10 million objects. We need to partition the data.
Shard A Shard B Shard C
Each shard maintains its own hash map and linked list and eviction structure
This has a problem when new shards are added. It will move huge precentage
of keys to different servers/shard. This creates massive cache miss.
Use Consistant Hashing: place servers/shard on a hash ring
When new shard is added, only a portion of keys need to move
Suppose the application requests: GET user:123
Cache-aside-pattern: Also known as lazy loading
1. Read Path: The app checks the cache for the item. If found (cache hit), it returns the data
immediately. If not found (cache miss), the app queries the primary database, stores the result in the
cache, and returns it to the client.
2. Write Path: The app updates the primary database first and then explicitly invalidates or deletes
the corresponding key from the cache to prevent stale reads
• Resource Efficiency: Only data that is actually requested gets loaded into memory ("lazy" loading),
• High Resilience: If the cache layer goes down, the application continues to function by falling back
Why Not Maintain a Global LRU?
Every GET would have to somehow update a globally coordinated ordering:
With millions of requests/sec, that metadata becomes a synchronization bottleneck.
Suppose a celebrity profile receives 1 million req/sec. Consistant hashing sends
the request for that key to the same shard. That shard becomes overloaded.
Solution includes replicating hot keys, adding an L1 local cache, request coalescing,
Another major problem occurs when a popular key expires.

requests comes in so we miss the cache and hit database. This is a
Solution: Use request coalescing/single-flight: Only one request loads the value
DB also has the same information.
But later user changed its name in DB we will have to invalidate the data in cache.
I generally prefer invalidate-on-write over trying to manually synchronize every cached copy.
